item.title: Local govt elections: Voting in 1,026 union parishads in first phase
item.description:
The Election Commission (EC) plans to hold elections to more than 4,000 union parishads (UPs) in five phases, with voting in 1,026 UPs under 131 upazilas in the first phase on 21 January.

The EC took decisions on how many union parishads would go to polls in each phase at a meeting of the Election Commission at the Election Building in Agargaon, Dhaka, on Monday.

Later, Election Commissioner Abul Fazal Md Sanaullah briefed journalists on the decisions taken at the meeting. He said the list showing the election dates for each union parishads would be published on the EC website by next Thursday.

The election commissioner said voting is planned in 1,113 union parishads under 129 upazilas in the second phase, 1,002 union parishads under 118 upazilas in the third phase, 793 union parishads under 93 upazilas in the fourth phase and 356 union parishads under 37 upazilas in the fifth phase.

Dialogue with political parties in December

The Election Commission will hold a dialogue with political parties ahead of the union parishad elections. The EC plans to complete the dialogue before 10 December, Election Commissioner Abul Fazal said.

Abul Fazl said the issue of holding dialogue with political parties was discussed at the commission meeting. The parties will be invited for discussions over three days, in order of their registration, either towards the end of this month or at the beginning of December. The dialogue will be held before 10 December.

Asked whether any political party had demanded the deployment of the army in local government elections, Abul Fazl said the commission had not received any such demand yet.

Abul Fazal said the EC would consider the availability and effectiveness of law enforcement agencies during the union parishad elections. Necessary measures would be taken based on whether the relevant forces could effectively perform their duties in a particular area and maintain the election environment, he added.

Software complications in smart card printing

The commission meeting also discussed ongoing problems with National Identity Card (NID) services and smart card printing. Abul Fazal said the software used for smart card printing had been experiencing problems over the past four to five days.

However, he claimed that no NID services had been suspended because of this. He added that efforts were underway to resolve the issue.

After the meeting, it was announced that Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs) would no longer be used in any election. The commission meeting also discussed the progress of a committee formed to determine how the EVMs currently in storage would be disposed of.

Abul Fazal said, “A committee was formed to determine the disposal of these EVMs. The commission received an update on the progress of the committee's work today.”

Asked about environmental concerns and financial losses associated with destroying the EVMs, Abul Fazal said these issues had not yet been discussed by the commission. The committee's recommendations would have to be received first.

The election commissioner said there were several methods of destroying EVMs.

The method to be adopted would become clear once the relevant committee submitted its recommendations.

item.title: BGB patrols Gopalganj with armoured vehicles and body-worn cameras
item.description:
Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) and police have been patrolling Gopalganj since Monday morning to keep the law and order normal.

Police officers are stationed at various key intersections and in front of important establishments across the town.

No processions by leaders and activists of the Awami League, whose activities are banned, have been seen till noon.

In a statement sent from its headquarters, the BGB said 10 platoons have been deployed in key areas of Gopalganj district to maintain normal law and order and ensure public safety.

The necessary number of armoured personnel carriers (APCs) has also been deployed to deal with any untoward situation and to control riots.

The BGB said body-worn cameras have been attached to the largest possible number of deployed personnel to enable direct monitoring and coordination of their activities in the field. Live footage of operations on the ground is also being collected and monitored using drones and other technologies.

Gopalganj unrest: Govt warns of tough action if Awami League creates disorder
Following Sunday's violence, arson and vandalism, the overall law and order situation in Gopalganj returned to normal today, Monday. Government and private offices, courts and business establishments in the district reopened.

The BGB headquarters’ monitoring cell is closely overseeing these activities and the overall security situation so that necessary measures can be taken swiftly in the event of any untoward incident.

The BGB said its personnel have been deployed at key locations across the district under the ‘In Aid to Civil Power’ framework, following instructions from the Ministry of Home Affairs and in accordance with the requirements and advice of the district magistrate.

In coordination with other law enforcement agencies, they are monitoring the overall security situation and taking necessary measures to ensure the safety of the public and their property.

Situation under control

Following Sunday's violence, arson and vandalism, the overall law and order situation in Gopalganj returned to normal today, Monday. Government and private offices, courts and business establishments in the district reopened.

Traffic was also moving normally on the Dhaka-Khulna Highway and on the roads within the district town.

Govt monitors Gopalganj situation, considers action based on developments

At around 10:30 am on Monday, members of law enforcement agencies were seen on duty in various parts of Gopalganj town, including Bankpara intersection, the area around the deputy commissioner's residence, the launch terminal, Jugshikha intersection, Thana Para intersection, the district court, the hospital, Police Lines intersection and Bedgram.

Sunday’s events had disrupted the daily lives of ordinary people. Although businesses in the town reopened today, some fear remains among local traders and transport workers.

Fruit trader Tarikul Islam said, “I bought fruit yesterday but could not sell it. I am always worried about when a protest might break out and when I might have to close my shop.”

Rickshaw puller Enamul Haque said his home was in Kalia upazila of Narail. He had been driving a rickshaw in Gopalganj for seven years.

During yesterday's incident, he did not take his rickshaw out for two to three hours. He later went out in the afternoon. He said he had been driving as usual since this morning and has faced no problems.

Md Aminul Islam, OC, Gopalganj Sadar police station No untoward incidents have been reported anywhere so far. The law and order situation in the district remained normal.

Asked whether the BNP would announce any programme in response to yesterday's violence, Gopalganj district BNP convener Sharif Rafiquzzaman told Prothom Alo that no decision has yet been made. A decision would be taken after discussions with the party's central leaders.

Earlier, between 11:00 am and 1:45 pm on Sunday, leaders and activists of the Awami League staged processions along various roads in Gopalganj town. Many of them were carrying locally made weapons, including oars, sticks, machetes, Chinese axes, spears and lances.

During the processions, a police armoured personnel carrier (APC) and a police box were vandalised. The leaders and activists of the party also vandalised the plaque bearing the name of July Memorial and Hadi Chattar.

On Sunday evening, the residence of Imdadul Haque Mollah, president of Tungipara municipal BNP unit, was set on fire. Later that evening, miscreants attacked police Sub-Inspector Moslem Ali with sharp weapons in Tungipara, leaving him injured.

Gopalganj DC, SP removed from their posts

Moslem Ali is the complainant in a case filed over the vandalism and arson of a police vehicle in Tungipara. Violence and vandalism took place throughout the day in Gopalganj on 10 November. On that day, leaders and activists of the Awami League set fire to a police vehicle.

In response to the situation, officers-in-charge (OCs) of three police stations in the district were transferred Sunday night. They are Tungipara police station OC Md Ayub Ali, Kotalipara police station OC Riyad Mahmud and Kashiani police station OC Mahfuzur Rahman. All three have been transferred to Kishoreganj district.

Earlier, on Sunday afternoon, Gopalganj Deputy Commissioner Md Arif-Uz-Zaman and Police Superintendent Md Habibullah were transferred as well.

Asked about the law and order situation in Gopalganj, Sadar police station OC Md Aminul Islam said no untoward incidents have been reported anywhere so far. The law and order situation in the district remained normal.

No case had been filed in connection with Sunday’s violence by Monday noon. No one has been detained or arrested over the incident either, Gopalganj Sadar police station OC Aminul Islam said.

item.title: Ton-up Litton, lower order power Bangladesh to 400, pile pressure on South Africa
item.description:
TOPSHOT-CRICKET-RSA-BAN-TEST

Bangladesh were bowled out for 400 in their first innings on the second day of the first Test against South Africa in Johannesburg on Monday, posting a formidable total after a remarkable recovery from a disastrous start.

Resuming at 327 for 6, Bangladesh added 73 runs to their overnight total before losing their remaining four wickets. Litton Das completed his eighth Test century, scoring 120 off 179 balls, while some hitting from the lower order helped the visitors reach the 400-run mark.

Kagiso Rabada claimed five wickets, while Dane Paterson took four for the hosts.

Litton, who had been unbeaten on 92 overnight, reached his century in the fourth over of the morning.

He struck Marco Jansen for a boundary to bring up the milestone, then celebrated by raising his bat and helmet and taking a note from his pocket.

The message was dedicated to his daughter, Anayra, who turned three on Monday: "Happy birthday, my princess. This 100 is for you."

His innings ended at 120 when he attempted to pull a short delivery from Dane Paterson and was caught at short midwicket. Bangladesh were then 374 for 8.

Mehidy Hasan Miraz was the first wicket to fall on the second morning, caught at first slip off Dane Paterson for 10. Litton's dismissal was followed by Hasan Mahmud, who edged a Paterson delivery to the wicketkeeper for 2, leaving Bangladesh at 392 for 9.

Taskin Ahmed took Bangladesh to the 400-run mark with a boundary off Paterson but was dismissed off the next delivery, caught by Mulder, bringing the innings to an end.

The total was particularly significant at the Wanderers Stadium, where no team has ever lost a Test match after posting more than 320 in the first innings. Teams making over 320 have won 12 times and drawn seven matches at the Johannesburg venue.

Bangladesh's innings was built around a remarkable 206-run sixth-wicket partnership between Towhid Hridoy and Litton. Hridoy scored 137 on the opening day before being dismissed off the final delivery, while Litton carried on to complete his century the following morning.

The partnership rescued Bangladesh after they had slumped to 22 for 3 early in the innings and later lost their fifth wicket at 108. Hridoy and Litton's stand became Bangladesh's highest partnership against South Africa in Test cricket.

Bangladesh's 400 also marked their highest total against South Africa in Test cricket, giving the visitors a strong platform.

item.title: Visiting the parliament from the village, Meherin and Shimana set higher goals
item.description:
Meherin Khandaker used to travel four kilometres every day from her village in remote Jongra to attend college in Patgram, Lalmonirhat, about 450 kilometres from Dhaka. Frequent power outages in the village disrupted her studies at night, so she would wake up early to finish her lessons in daylight.

Overcoming these and other challenges, Meherin secured GPA-5 in the HSC examinations from the humanities group at Punam Chand Bhutoria College in Patgram. She had secured the exact same result in her SSC exams as well.

Her achievement opened the door to an opportunity that took her beyond the hardships of rural life. Last Sunday, she stood in front of the Jatiya Sangsad Bhaban, the national parliament building in Dhaka. Excited to see in person what she had read about in textbooks, Meherin said she had long wanted to learn how the country's legislature functions.

"I was very eager to see how the country's legislature operates. Today, that wish has come true," she said after visiting the parliament building. Meherin is particularly interested in studying political science.

She was among 41 meritorious students from Patgram and Hatibandha upazilas who secured GPA-5 in the HSC examinations and visited the capital. Besides touring the Jatiya Sangsad Bhaban, they paid a courtesy call on Prime Minister Tarique Rahman. For the students from these remote areas, the trip was an entirely new experience.

Another member of the group was Sharmin Akter Shimana from Hatibandha. She secured GPA-5 in the humanities group at Alimuddin Government College and is now preparing for university admission tests. She dreams of studying English language and literature at the University of Dhaka. She also hopes to pursue higher studies at the University of Cambridge after completing her undergraduate degree in Bangladesh.

Shimana was captivated by the parliament building. "I had read about this remarkable structure designed by Louis I Kahn in books. Today, I saw it in person. The building looks complete from every angle. The green water of the lake alongside such a vast structure fascinated me," she said.

Yamin Bin Asad Mahin, another student of Alimuddin Government College, was also part of the group. Inspired by his father, a college teacher, Mahin secured GPA-5 in the humanities group in both his SSC and HSC examinations. His immediate goal is to gain admission to the University of Dhaka.

Recalling his visit to the parliament building and meeting with the prime minister, Mahin said, "Coming from a remote area, getting to see such a grand arrangement is a great source of inspiration for us. It will give us confidence as we face the challenges ahead."

Behind the achievements of these students from Patgram and Hatibandha are stories of perseverance amid various limitations. Difficulties in commuting and other challenges of living in remote areas could not hold back their aspirations.

Local MP Barrister Hasan Rajib Pradhan supervised the students throughout the educational tour.

Speaking about their achievements, Hasan Rajib Pradhan said, "Hatibandha and Patgram are about 450 kilometres from Dhaka. Our students are doing well despite numerous challenges. We will continue to support them so that they can complete their education without interruption in the future."

item.title: From patient-centered care to physician-enabled patient care
item.description:
Throughout my experience in hospital management, I have observed an important relationship that is sometimes overlooked in healthcare management: while the patient is the ultimate recipient and beneficiary of healthcare services, the physician is one of the most critical professional stakeholders through whom the quality of patient care is delivered.

Hospitals traditionally emphasize the principle that “the patient is our customer.” This is absolutely correct from the perspective of patient experience, service quality, safety, satisfaction, and clinical outcomes. However, hospital management must also recognise that excellent patient care does not happen in isolation. It is delivered through a complex ecosystem involving physicians, nurses, technicians, pharmacists, administrators, support services, technology, infrastructure, and numerous operational processes. 

Within this ecosystem, physicians occupy a particularly important position because they are directly involved in clinical decision-making, diagnosis, treatment planning, coordination of care, and communication with patients and their families.

Therefore, an important management principle can be stated as: “If we want to create an excellent patient experience, we must first create an environment in which physicians and healthcare professionals can deliver their best.”

A fundamental principle of hospital management can be expressed as: “Patient-centered care is the destination; physician enablement is one of the most important pathways to reach it.”

The physician as a critical internal customer

From a hospital management perspective, physicians can be viewed as critical internal customers or professional partners.

Their needs may include:

  • Appropriate clinical facilities and infrastructure

  • Availability of medicines, equipment, and diagnostic services

  • Reliable laboratory and imaging support

  • Competent nursing and allied healthcare teams

  • Efficient appointment and scheduling systems

  • Timely access to clinical information and medical records

  • Effective IT and hospital information systems

  • Appropriate administrative support

  • Clear clinical and operational protocols

  • Efficient billing and insurance processes

  • Professional respect and autonomy within appropriate governance

  • Timely communication and decision-making

  • Adequate support for emergencies and critical cases

  • Opportunities for professional development and academic activities

  • A safe, ethical, and professionally supportive working environment

When these requirements are systematically addressed, physicians are better positioned to concentrate on what they do best—providing safe, effective, compassionate, and evidence-based clinical care.

The Service Chain: Management → Physician → Patient

This creates an important service chain:

Effective Hospital Management ↓ Physician Enablement & Engagement ↓ Better Clinical Decision-Making & Care Delivery ↓ Better Patient Experience & Clinical Outcomes

In this model, hospital management's role is not simply to "manage the hospital." Its deeper responsibility is to remove barriers that prevent healthcare professionals from delivering excellent care.

A physician who has the right information, resources, support services, infrastructure, technology, and competent team can devote greater attention to the patient.

Conversely, when physicians constantly face operational problems—missing equipment, delayed investigations, inadequate nursing support, inefficient processes, poor communication, administrative obstacles, or unreliable systems—the consequences can eventually reach the patient.

Therefore, Patient-Centered Care Begins Behind the Patient

One of the most important lessons from hospital management is that patient-centered care is not created only at the patient's bedside.

It begins behind the scenes. It begins with:

Good Governance → Good Systems → Good Processes → Enabled Healthcare Professionals → Consistent Clinical Service → Excellent Patient Experience

The patient sees only the final part of this chain. Hospital management, however, must manage the entire chain.

The concept of "physician-enabled patient care"

The philosophy does not replace patient-centered care. Instead, it strengthens it.

The patient remains the ultimate focus of the hospital, while physicians and other healthcare professionals become critical enablers of that patient-centered mission.

This leads to a broader management equation:

Patient-Centered Care = Patient Focus + Physician Enablement + Teamwork + Process Excellence + Organisational Support

A three-level customer perspective

Hospital management can therefore consider three interconnected levels:

LEVEL 1 — The Patient The ultimate recipient and beneficiary of healthcare services.

LEVEL 2 — The Physician & Healthcare Professional The critical internal stakeholder who requires the right environment, resources, systems, and support to deliver quality care.

LEVEL 3 — Hospital Management The enabler that designs the systems, provides resources, removes barriers, establishes governance, and creates the environment in which healthcare professionals can perform effectively.

This produces a powerful principle: “Take care of the people who take care of the patients.”

And in a hospital, taking care of those who take care of patients means much more than employee welfare. It means providing them with the systems, resources, information, infrastructure, authority, support, and organisational environment necessary to perform their professional responsibilities effectively.

The ultimate objective

The ultimate objective is not to create a hospital where physicians are satisfied at the expense of patients. Nor is it to focus exclusively on patients while ignoring the professionals responsible for their care.

The objective is to create an integrated care ecosystem in which the interests of patients, physicians, nurses, allied health professionals, and the organisation are aligned.

When hospital management understands and responds effectively to the legitimate professional needs of physicians, it creates the conditions for physicians to deliver better care.

And when physicians are enabled to deliver better care, patients receive better care.

Therefore, a fundamental principle of hospital management can be expressed as: “Patient-centered care is the destination; physician enablement is one of the most important pathways to reach it.”

This perspective shifts hospital management from simply asking: “What do our patients need?” to also asking: “What do our physicians and healthcare professionals need from us so that they can consistently provide what our patients need?”

That is where strategic hospital management, physician engagement, operational excellence, and patient experience come together.

* Md. Nawshad Pervez is Group Executive Director- Human Resources, United Group

item.title: TOP SHOTS (16 November 2026)
Deleted from India's voter rolls, some Muslims face detention, deportation
item.description:
INDIA-POLITICS/CITIZENSHIP

  • Voter-roll exclusions raise citizenship fears in India

  • Muslims describe detention after names vanish from rolls

  • Home Minister Shah links removal from voter rolls to expelling migrants

  • Court petitions challenge Fakir, others' deportation, detentions

  • Families cite decades of records to prove Indian roots

When Sahida Fakir stepped out of her Mumbai home on 19 July to buy vegetables, she told her younger son she would be back in minutes.

More than three months later, the 38-year-old is living in a Bangladeshi village, separated from her husband and two sons.

Fakir said plainclothes officers detained her, seized her phone — which she said contained copies of identity documents — and eventually forced her across the border. Court filings show the officials belonged to the Mumbai police crime branch. The department did not respond to a request for comment.

"Someone grabbed my hand from behind and ordered me to get into the vehicle," Fakir told Reuters in Satkhira, Bangladesh.

Fakir is among 10 families Reuters interviewed whose relatives were detained, deported or questioned over their citizenship after being dropped from India's revised electoral rolls. All had Indian identity or family documents while relatives including parents and siblings remained on the voter lists.

The cases show how India's sweeping voter-roll revision has become entangled with a separate drive to identify and expel suspected illegal immigrants, even though removal from the rolls does not itself establish that someone is a foreigner.

The voter list revision struck 130 million names nationwide in the largest deletion of voters in India's history. Data shows the omissions disproportionately affect Muslims, India's largest minority, who have faced what rights groups describe as exclusionarypolicies and rising discrimination since Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party took power in 2014.

The revision sparked massive protests and accusations that the BJP was reshaping the electorate in its favour. The party denies targeting legitimate citizens.

In West Bengal, where it has run furthest, around 9 million names were cut ahead of state elections earlier this year. Muslims made up about 70 per cent of the 2.7 million names deleted after a closer review, despite being 27 per cent of the population, according to the Kolkata-based Sabar Institute.

The BJP emerged victorious in those polls and took control of the state for the first time.

"We cannot deny the anti-incumbency factor but the voter deletions played a big role in determining West Bengal election results," the institute's founder, Sabir Ahamed, said.

Voter Rolls and Expulsions

Home Minister Amit Shah explicitly linked the two at a 5 November rally in the northern state of Haryana.

"It is the BJP's resolve that we will detect infiltrators, remove them from the electoral rolls, and after that, we will pick them out one by one and expel them from the country," Shah said.

West Bengal has been a major flashpoint for crackdowns primarily on Bengali-speaking Muslims.

Citizenship and migration carry particular weight in the state, where the border drawn by the British when India was partitioned in 1947 split the region into two. Millions crossed during the upheaval and again during Bangladesh's 1971 independence war, leaving families and communities straddling the frontier.

India's Home Ministry, Prime Minister's Office and Election Commission did not respond to a request for comment.

Court Battles

Fakir said she was pushed into Bangladesh at 1:00 am from an unmanned, unfenced stretch of the border. Caked in mud, she said she walked for hours before a farmer found her crying and took her in.

Mumbai police told the court she was handed to the Border Security Force on the Assam border and "subsequently deported to Bangladesh through the designated authorities." Bangladesh's border force, home and foreign affairs ministries and Prime Minister's Office did not respond to a request for comment.

Court filings show Fakir was among 149 people deported during that operation, after being identified by authorities as Bangladeshi nationals.

"I never imagined, not even for a moment, that they would send me to Bangladesh," Fakir said. "My home, my grandparents and my entire family lineage are rooted in India."

Now her husband, Jumman, is fighting her case in court, alongside millions of challenges to West Bengal's voter-roll revision.

A petition filed by her family in the Supreme Court in August argued that deletion from the electoral roll could not determine citizenship and that she could not be removed on the basis of an "untested executive assertion."

Family records reviewed by Reuters show Fakir's parents and grandparents were registered voters in Swarupnagar, West Bengal, from India's first national election in 1952. Their names also appeared on the 2002-03 rolls, a benchmark in the latest revision for determining who could remain without submitting additional documents.

Fakir herself has appeared on West Bengal's electoral rolls since at least 2008, according to her voter ID seen by Reuters.

Mumbai's Foreigners Regional Registration Office told the Calcutta High Court that Fakir produced a Bangladeshi birth certificate during an inquiry and failed to produce "valid or credible documentary evidence" establishing Indian citizenship.

Fakir disputed that, saying authorities seized her phone and gave her no opportunity to show copies of documents stored on it. Indian law does not require citizens to carry valid identification at all times.

‘You are a Bangladeshi’

In another petition before the Calcutta High Court, utensil hawker Nasiruddin Sheikh and four others said they were detained after their names were removed from the rolls, even though appeals against deletion were pending before special tribunals.

Sheikh said police detained him and 22 others while he was working hundreds of kilometres from home in Chhattisgarh. Nineteen were released after 14 days when authorities found their names on revised rolls, he said. Sheikh and three others whose names did not appear remained in custody for 32 days.

"A policeman told me, 'Your name is not in the voter list. You are a Bangladeshi,'" Sheikh said.

He was released with the others the night before their court hearing. Sheikh said their detention centre had a large hall with beds for more than 60 people. Detainees underwent medical examinations and biometric registration before confinement.

"It was a jail in every sense. We couldn't go outside," he said.

Police and state lawyers have told the Calcutta High Court that West Bengal has no permanent detention camps.

At a holding centre for suspected foreign migrants in Murshidabad, Reuters reporters saw clothes hanging inside and people peering from windows. An ambulance and a covered police bus stood within the heavily guarded compound.

Mosami Ray, who lives opposite, said she saw people brought there two months ago and families weeping outside.

"There are millions of cases against deletion of names from voter list and people are waiting for justice," human rights activist Kirity Roy said. "The tribunals are slow. We are hopeless with what is going on."

item.title: Gopalganj procession reaches Pirojpur, 2 BNP offices attacked
item.description:
Two Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) offices in Nazirpur upazila of Pirojpur were attacked, vandalised and set on fire. Meanwhile, stones and brickbats were thrown at the house of a BNP leader in the upazila’s Malikhali union.

Several eyewitnesses alleged that leaders and activists of the Awami League, whose activities are banned, arrived in a procession from Gopalganj and carried out the attacks.

The incidents took place yesterday, Sunday afternoon, at the Mobile Tower intersection in Uttar Jhanjhania area of Malikhali union in the upazila.

Gopalganj unrest: Govt warns of tough action if Awami League creates disorder

According to local sources, the scene of the incident in Nazirpur’s Uttar Jhanjhania is around 10–12 kilometres from Tungipara upazila in neighbouring Gopalganj district. A group of around 350 people travelled from Tungipara to the Mobile Tower intersection in Uttar Jhanjhania in various vehicles, including pickup trucks.

They first went to the house of Suman Talukder, joint convener of Malikhali union BNP, and threw stones and brickbats at it. One of the house’s Thai glass panels was broken. They then vandalised a BNP office beside the Mobile Tower intersection and set it on fire.

Awami League leaders visit Bangabandhu's mausoleum in Tungipara after 2.5 years

Another office, belonging to Motaleb Hossain, a joint convener of Malikhali union BNP, was also attacked. Chairs and tables kept inside the office were broken, taken outside and set on fire. Parts of the office’s tin structure were also damaged with sharp weapons.

Pirojpur district BNP Member Secretary Saidul Islam Kismat said legal action would be taken over the incident.

However, Nazirpur police station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Tarikul Islam said no complaint has been received as of Monday morning. He said appropriate action would be taken if a complaint was filed.

Is Awami League’s current politics self-destructive, or an attempt to seek an opportunity?

item.title: Is Awami League’s current politics self-destructive, or an attempt to seek an opportunity?
item.description:
More than two years after losing power, the Awami League has once again become a subject of public discussion because of its recent activities. Flash processions, the detonation of crude bombs, and the setting of buses on fire have all sparked considerable debate.

But can we really understand what the party is trying to achieve simply by looking at these incidents? Why has its style of politics taken this turn after governing the country for so many years? Rather than seeking definitive answers to these questions, let us try to understand these developments more deeply through several different hypotheses.

First hypothesis: Are old calculations still at play?

After spending fifteen and a half years in power, do Awami League leaders and activists still consider running the country their rightful role? Are they hoping to return by relying on their old connections with the administration, police, business community, and influential figures? Is there a calculation that creating instability could open up opportunities for bargaining?

Indonesia’s President Suharto stepped down in 1998 following mass protests, after ruling the country for 31 years. However, his Golkar Party remained in the country, maintained its organisational structure, and subsequently participated in elections. In Bangladesh, even after the assassination of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman in 1975 and, later, the killing of the four national leaders, other Awami League leaders, including Zohra Tajuddin, remained in the country and tried to rebuild the party.

Is the situation after 5 August 2024, similar to either of these two earlier episodes? Many Awami League leaders and activists, from the central leadership to the grassroots, including Sheikh Hasina herself, have left the country or gone into hiding.

Does the Awami League believe that if an opportunity arises to re-enter the political arena, it will be able to demonstrate its strength on the streets? But given its past record of repression, arrests, and obstructing elections against opposition parties while in power, would the BNP, Jamaat, and other political parties be willing to give it that opportunity?

Another question concerns the fact that, after being in power for so long, many people's personal interests became intertwined with the Awami League. Some benefited in business, others secured jobs or government contracts, while some wielded influence in their localities. Political scientists Herbert Kitschelt and Steven Wilkinson, in their edited volume Patrons, Clients and Policies, show how political relationships are built not only around ideology but also through the exchange of benefits and privileges. This phenomenon is known as clientelism.

So, are the Awami League's former beneficiaries working towards the party's future, or are they simply hoping to regain the influence they have lost?

Second hypothesis: Does the fracturing of the july alliance present an opportunity for Awami League?

In July–August 2024, various political forces united against Awami League. However, following the fall of the government, disagreements emerged among BNP, Jamaat, and NCP over elections, reforms, and the governance of the country. Some may be disappointed with BNP, others may be critical of Jamaat, while still others may be dissatisfied with the activities of NCP. These issues are also being discussed on television talk shows. Does the Awami League believe that these divisions are creating an opportunity for its political comeback?

But does criticism of other political parties necessarily indicate support for the Awami League? In political psychology, confirmation bias refers to the tendency to give greater weight to information that aligns with one's existing beliefs. Are Awami League leaders also interpreting these criticisms as signs that the party is poised for a comeback?

Could developments surrounding the history and culture of the Liberation War also be reinforcing these hopes? The Dhanmondi 32 residence was demolished, ink was thrown on a portrait of Rabindranath Tagore, and shrines and dargahs belonging to people of various religious faiths came under attack. Yet many people from these very communities had also supported the July uprising.

Recently, in Cumilla, NCP leaders and activists demolished a nameplate bearing the name of an heir at the residence of martyred Dhirendranath Datta. They argued that the house should be turned into a museum rather than sold. Will people angered by such incidents turn towards the Awami League? Or are loving history and culture and supporting the Awami League two entirely separate things?

Does the Awami League also have similar calculations regarding religious minorities? Following the change of government, attacks were carried out on their homes, businesses, and places of worship. However, is the party also taking into account the generally positive experiences of Hindus during the most recent Durga Puja and the growing ties between some Hindu organisations and the BNP? Does the Awami League believe that a breakdown in these relationships will bring Hindus back to its fold?

Yet Hindus also faced attacks and persecution during the Awami League's own tenure. Does having concerns about their security necessarily mean they will support the Awami League?

But even amid political divisions, have people forgotten the loss of life and the repression during the July uprising? According to a 2025 report by the United Nations Human Rights Office, approximately 1,400 people may have been killed between July 2024 and 15 August 2024. The report also documents serious human rights violations allegedly committed by the former government's security forces and groups affiliated with the Awami League.

Does the Awami League believe that these memories will fade with time? In political psychology, collective memory refers to the lasting impact of major events on a society's shared consciousness, which can also influence political decisions in the future. Does the party understand the enduring power of the memories of July?

Third hypothesis: Reliance on India, or an opportunity arising from global developments?

To what extent is reliance on India shaping the Awami League's current political strategy? The Sheikh Hasina government maintained close relations with India for many years. Do party leaders still believe that India will stand by them? A political party that believes it has powerful friends abroad may be willing to take significant risks. Has the Awami League received any new assurances, or is it moving forward on the strength of its longstanding relationship with India? Is it also taking India's own interests into consideration?

Meanwhile, global politics remains turbulent, with the war involving Iran, the crisis in the Middle East, and tensions among major powers. Are some within the Awami League thinking that, with the world's attention focused elsewhere, an opportunity has emerged to intensify political activities in Bangladesh? But does reduced international media coverage of Bangladesh necessarily mean that foreign governments are paying less attention to the country? They, too, have interests in Bangladesh's stability, security, and economy.

Can people still be intimidated by flash processions and crude bomb explosions? Does Awami League believe that people will be frightened simply by witnessing these activities?

The economic consequences of war are also affecting ordinary people. Oil prices and transportation costs have risen in international markets. Fuel prices have also been increased in Bangladesh, putting additional pressure on transportation, production, and the cost of essential commodities. In such circumstances, if people begin to feel that "things were better before," does the Awami League interpret this as a sign that public support for the party is returning? But are dissatisfaction over the cost of living, assessments of the previous government, and preferences about who should govern the country in the future really the same thing?

Fourth hypothesis: Overconfidence, or a misreading of reality?

How much accurate information about the situation in the country are Awami League leaders receiving since losing power? From abroad, they watch videos of the party's processions and read comments from supporters on Facebook. People around them may also be reporting only positive developments. All this could create the impression that better days are returning for the party. But are the leaders hearing the views of those who remain silent?

In psychology, there is a concept known as an echo chamber. Simply put, it means repeatedly hearing opinions that reinforce one's existing preferences. Psychologist Irving Janis, through his work on groupthink, demonstrated how, when everyone in a group tries to maintain consensus, dissenting opinions and warnings about potential dangers tend to be overlooked. This can lead to a distorted perception of one's own strength.

Has Awami League's leadership now reached a point where it places greater trust in the opinions of its own supporters?

Moreover, not all Awami League leaders and activists have the same objectives. Some want to pursue politics based on the ideals of Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, some want to keep the party alive, while others want to retain their leadership positions in their localities. Banners at the party's flash processions also feature photographs of local leaders alongside Sheikh Hasina. Are these individuals working for the party, or are they trying to prevent someone else from taking their place?

In political science, the principal-agent problem refers to situations in which the interests of central leadership and grassroots activists do not always align. So, are these processions being organised at the direction of the central leadership, or are local leaders simply trying to preserve their own positions? Do leaders living abroad understand this distinction?

Fifth hypothesis: How far can politics of power display go?

Political scientists Andrew Kydd and Barbara Walter, in their research on The Strategies of Terrorism, have shown how an organisation can use violence to demonstrate its strength and put pressure on a government. Sending such a message by taking significant risks is known as costly signalling. They also describe as provocation the strategy of attempting to provoke a government into harsh repression in order to gain public sympathy.

Could similar calculations be behind the Awami League's flash processions, crude bomb explosions, and arson attacks? Are they trying to intimidate the government, embolden their own activists, or convey the message that it is difficult to conduct the country's politics without them?

Banned Awami League activists stage armed rally, vandalise property in Gopalganj

But after witnessing the bloodshed of July-August 2024 and the deaths of so many people, including children and adolescents, can people still be intimidated by flash processions and crude bomb explosions? Does Awami League believe that people will be frightened simply by witnessing these activities? Or is the party failing to take into account how much public sentiment has changed since the mass uprising?

In politics, people often regard violence committed by their own party as an act of courage, while condemning the same actions when committed by their opponents as criminal. In their book Radical American Partisanship, American political scientists Nathan Kalmoe and Lilliana Mason demonstrate how blind loyalty to one's political party can fuel hatred towards political opponents and increase support for violence.

Another American political scientist, Sean Westwood, and his fellow researchers, in their study Correcting Misperceptions of Political Violence, show that actual public support for political violence may be considerably lower than people perceive it to be. So, even if a party activist considers detonating a crude bomb an act of courage, would that same person accept killing people by setting a bus on fire?

However, violence can also produce the opposite of its intended effect. In 1998, a bombing by the Real IRA, an armed separatist organisation in Northern Ireland, killed 29 people. Among the victims were a pregnant woman and her unborn twins. The attack triggered widespread public outrage. What would happen in Bangladesh if ordinary people were killed in crude bomb explosions or in fires set to police vehicles or buses?

The Awami League has been promoting a narrative that hundreds of police officers were killed at the hands of participants in the July uprising. If police officers are killed through the party's own acts of violence, would that not undermine the credibility of this narrative? Similarly, would it not call into question the party's longstanding allegations that the BNP and Jamaat were responsible for setting buses on fire in 2013–15? In trying to demonstrate its strength, could the party end up weakening its own position?

The final word

In politics, the consequences of miscalculation are not borne by political leaders alone; ordinary people also pay the price. Does Awami League understand that the path it sees as a route back to power could, in fact, become an even greater obstacle to its return?

* Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder is a teacher and researcher in the Department of Political Science and Sociology at North South University

item.title: Worker injured in attack during Savar labour unrest dies in hospital
item.description:
A worker injured in an attack by outsiders in Savar, Dhaka, has died while undergoing treatment. His family said he died at around 3:00 am early on Monday, while receiving treatment in the intensive care unit (ICU) of Dhaka Medical College Hospital.

The deceased worker was Md Selim, 23, son of Mohammad Rahim of Kanaipur village in Kalkini upazila of Madaripur. He worked as a junior operator at a factory called Trent Shoes Ltd in the Aukpara area of Savar.

Selim was injured in an attack by outsiders in the Aukpara area on 4 November, amid labour unrest over various demands, including raising the minimum wage to Tk 30,000. As of today, Monday, police have arrested four people in connection with a case filed over the incident.

Garment workers’ minimum wage board meeting postponed

Family members of Selim and factory officials said workers were on duty at Trent Shoes Ltd, a leather goods manufacturer in the Aukpara area, on 4 November. At the time, a group of outsiders attacked several factories in the surrounding area. In response to the situation, the factory, along with other establishments, announced a holiday at around 12:30 pm that day.

Selim was standing beside the road as workers were leaving the factory. Suddenly, a man struck him on the head with an object resembling an iron rod. The attackers also beat two other workers at the factory, Md Rakib, 24, and Limon, 25.

How much will garment manufacturers offer in minimum wages?

Selim, who was seriously injured, was first taken to Enam Medical College Hospital, a private hospital in Savar. He was later taken to the National Institute of Neurosciences and Hospital in Dhaka before being admitted to Dhaka Medical College Hospital. He died at around 3:00 am today while undergoing treatment in the ICU there.

An official of Trent Shoes Ltd told Prothom Alo that Selim had remained unconscious since he was injured. The factory had made every effort to save him, but ultimately he could not be saved. The other two workers injured in the attack have recovered.

Confirming that a case was filed at Ashulia police station on 7 November, Dhaka Additional Superintendent of Police (Savar Circle) Rakibul Hasan told Prothom Alo that four people, including the main accused in the case, Ranjit Biswas, had been arrested.

item.title: Govt approves 2 new police stations, 2 municipalities
item.description:
The government has approved the formation of two new police stations and two municipalities to make administrative activities across the country more dynamic and public service-oriented.

At the same time, it has been decided to rename a police station and relocate the administrative headquarters of two upazilas.

The proposals were approved at a meeting of the National Implementation Committee for Administrative Reorganisation (NICAR) of Bangladesh on Monday. Prime Minister Tarique Rahman chaired the meeting.

Under the approved decisions, Matamuhuri Police Station will be established in Bottoli area of Konakhali Union under Matamuhuri Upazila by dividing Chakaria Police Station in Cox’s Bazar district.

The government has also approved the establishment of Mokamtala Police Station in the newly formed Mokamtala Upazila by dividing Shibganj Police Station in Bogura district.

The meeting also approved proposals to establish Mokamtala Municipality in Mokamtala Upazila of Bogura district and Jaintapur Municipality in Jaintapur Upazila of Sylhet district.

Meanwhile, Pagla Police Station in the newly formed Dakshin Gafargaon Upazila of Mymensingh district will be renamed Dakshin Gafargaon Police Station to bring its name in line with that of the upazila.

The government has also approved relocating the administrative headquarters of the newly formed Chandraganj Upazila, created by dividing Sadar Upazila in Lakshmipur district.

Instead of the previously proposed Motobi and Charchamita mouzas, the new headquarters will be established in Mouza No. 163 Uttar Chandrapur and Mouza No. 166 Hajirpara, under Hajirpara Union.

Similarly, the administrative headquarters of the newly formed Bangra Upazila, created by dividing Muradnagar Upazila in Cumilla district, will be relocated from Khamargram Mouza to Mouza No. 40 Dakshin Bangra under Bangra Purba Union.

According to relevant sources, the proposals to establish new police stations and rename an existing one were submitted by the Ministry of Home Affairs.

The proposals to form new municipalities and relocate upazila administrative headquarters were submitted by the Local Government Division.

Once implemented, the decisions will create a new administrative structure in the areas concerned, affecting administrative activities, law and order maintenance and the delivery of public services at the local level.

item.title: 44 organisations receive the corporate governance excellence award
item.description:
The Institute of Chartered Secretaries of Bangladesh (ICSB) organised the 13th ICSB National Award for Corporate Governance Excellence, 2025 at the Grand Ballroom of Pan Pacific Sonargaon, Dhaka, recognising listed companies for their outstanding commitment to corporate governance, transparency, and accountability. The theme of the award was “Promoting Governing Excellence.”

The award recognised companies that demonstrated excellence in governance practices during the year 2025 in compliance with the Corporate Governance Codes of the Bangladesh Securities and Exchange Commission (BSEC) and relevant regulatory frameworks.

Khandakar Abdul Muktadir, honourable minister, Ministry of Commerce, Ministry of Textiles and Jute, and Ministry of Industries, Government of the People’s Republic of Bangladesh, graced the occasion as the chief guest.

The programme was further honoured by the presence of Hafiz Ahmed Chowdhury, Secretary, Legislative and Parliamentary Affairs Division, Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs; Sharf Uddin Ahmed Choudhury, Secretary, Ministry of Commerce; Masud Khan, FCA, FCMA, Chairman, Bangladesh Securities and Exchange Commission (BSEC) as Special Guests.

The ceremony was presided over by Mohammad Shahajahan FCS, President, ICSB Md Abdullah Al Mamun FCS, Chairman, Corporate Governance Committee, ICSB, presented the overview of the Corporate Governance Awarding Charter.

44 winning companies listed on the Dhaka Stock Exchange PLC and Chittagong Stock Exchange PLC were recognised under 14 different categories and were awarded Gold, Silver, and Bronze trophies. Chief Guest and Special Guests handed over the trophies and certificates among the winning companies.

BRAC Bank PLC and Eastern Bank PLC have jointly won the Gold trophy in the General Banking Companies category while City Bank PLC has secured silver and Pubali Bank PLC Bronze.

Shahjalal Islami Bank PLC has won the Gold award in the Islami Banking Companies category.

IDLC Finance PLC has won the Gold award in the Finance Companies category while DBH Finance PLC has bagged Silver and IPDC Finance PLC. has received Bronze award.

In the General Insurance Companies category, the Gold trophy have jointly won by City Insurance PLC & Sena Insurance PLC, the Silver has gone to Nitol Insurance PLC and the Bronze to Reliance Insurance PLC.

In the Life Insurance Companies category, Meghna Life Insurance PLC won Gold trophy, Chartered Life Insurance PLC has bagged Silver award while Pragati Life Insurance PLC received Bronze trophy.

The IBN SINA Pharmaceutical Industry PLC took home the top honor in the Pharmaceuticals and Chemicals Companies category Reckitt Benckiser (Bangladesh) PLC has won Silver and The ACME Laboratories Ltd. has received Bronze trophy.

In the Textiles and RMG Companies category, Paramount Textile PLC has bagged the Gold, Envoy Textiles Limited & Matin Spinning Mills PLC both have got Silver and Shasha Denims PLC has received Bronze trophy.

Unilever Consumer Care Limited has won Gold, Agricultural Marketing Co. Ltd has won Silver and Golden Harvest Agro Industries Ltd has won Bronze in the Food and Allied Companies category.

IT Consultants PLC has got the Gold trophy in the Information and Communication Technology Companies category while BDCOM Online Ltd has won Silver and ADN Telecom Limited has received Bronze trophy.

Walton Hi-Tech Industries PLC has got the Gold trophy in the Engineering Companies category, Bangladesh Steel Re-Rolling Mills Limited has won Silver and Rangpur Foundry Limited has won Bronze trophy.

Heidelberg Materials Bangladesh PLC has won the Gold, RAK Ceramics (Bangladesh) Limited has bagged Silver and Bata Shoe Company (Bangladesh) Limited & Crown Cement PLC. jointly received Bronze trophy in the Manufacturing Companies category.

In the Fuel and Power Companies category, MJL Bangladesh PLC. has secured Gold and United Power Generation & Distribution Company Ltd has received Silver trophy and Linde Bangladesh Limited has won Bronze trophy.

Eastern Housing Limited has won the Gold trophy in the Service Companies category while Unique Hotel & Resorts PLC has bagged Silver and Summit Alliance Port Limited has won Bronze trophy.

In the Telecommunications Companies category, Grameenphone Ltd. has bagged Gold award and Robi Axiata PLC. has received Silver and Bangladesh Submarine Cables PLC has secured Bronze trophy.

Speaking as the Chief Guest, Khandakar Abdul Muktadir said, “Good corporate governance is essential across all sectors to build a stronger and more sustainable economy.”

He appreciated ICSB’s efforts over the years to promote good governance by recognising companies that follow best practices. He also assured the Ministry of Commerce’s continued support for ICSB’s future activities and progress.

Hafiz Ahmed Chowdhury, Secretary, Legislative and Parliamentary Affairs Division, Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs, emphasised that corporate governance goes beyond regulatory compliance, reflecting an organisation’s values, leadership, and commitment to responsible business practices. He appreciated ICSB’s role in promoting transparency, accountability, and good governance in Bangladesh.

Sharf Uddin Ahmed Choudhury, Secretary, Ministry of Commerce, appreciated ICSB for putting efforts in promoting good governance and also for encouraging companies to uphold the standards of corporate governance. He also mentioned good governance is essential for sustainable economic growth. “

Masud Khan, FCA, FCMA, Chairman, Bangladesh Securities and Exchange Commission (BSEC), mentioned that good governance is essential for business operation. He also emphasised on balanced composition of boards, so that the stakeholder’s rights be protected. He mentioned ICSB as a as a true guardian of corporate governance. They carry a vital responsibility in ensuring these standards are practiced across the corporate sector.”

Earlier, in his Welcome Address, Mohammad Shahajahan, FCS, President of ICSB, called for a collective commitment to ensuring sound corporate governance, which is essential for the economic progress of our country.

Md Abdullah Al Mamun, FCS, Chairman of the Corporate Governance Committee, ICSB, outlined the evaluation process followed in selecting companies for the awards.

At the end, Md Rafiqul Islam FCS, Senior Vice President of ICSB thanked everyone on behalf of ICSB.

The programme was attended by dignitaries, government officials, eminent professionals, chairpersons, managing directors, directors, and senior officials from country’s leading corporate houses, along with members of the Institute and journalists. The guests commended ICSB's role in establishing governance in the Corporate Sector of Bangladesh and ensuring sustainable development.

What could be the mark distribution for 9th teachers’ recruitment examination?
item.description:
The Non-Government Teachers' Registration and Certification Authority (NTRCA) has proposed a total of 220 marks for the ninth teachers' recruitment examination, to be conducted in three stages.

The proposed distribution includes 100 marks each for the preliminary and written examinations, and 20 marks for the viva voce.

Preliminary examination: 100 marks across four subjects

According to the proposed syllabus, the preliminary examination will cover four subjects: Bangla, English, Mathematics and General Knowledge. Each subject may carry 25 marks, making the total 100 marks.

The examination is proposed to be conducted in a multiple-choice question (MCQ) format, with a duration of one hour.

Candidates will receive one mark for each correct answer, while 0.25 marks will be deducted for each incorrect answer. The proposed pass mark for the preliminary examination is 40 per cent.

Written and viva voce examination marks

Candidates who pass the preliminary examination will be eligible to sit the 100-mark written examination.

The written examination may last three hours. Candidates who pass this stage will then have to appear for a 20-mark viva voce examination.

However, these proposals regarding the examination method, mark distribution and syllabus have not yet been finalised. The authorities will confirm the details after amending the relevant regulations.

Recruitment circular may be published in December

According to NTRCA sources, viva voce examinations for the recruitment of heads of educational institutions and assistant heads are currently underway. These examinations are scheduled to conclude on 9 December.

The authority may then take initiatives to arrange the ninth teachers' recruitment examination. However, it will make a final decision on the examination only after receiving approval from the Ministry of Education.

item.title: Dhaka University admission: 5 steps to complete the application
item.description:
Applications are open for admission to Dhaka University’s (DU) undergraduate programmes for the 2026–27 academic year.

Prospective students are applying online, with the deadline set for 11:59pm on 25 November.

Admission tests for the academic year will be held under five units: Arts, Law and Social Sciences; Science; Business Studies; Fine Arts and IBA.

Students seeking admission to these units must follow several steps to complete their applications. The university has published detailed instructions on its admission website.

The application process involves five steps:

1. Login

Applicants must log in and provide the required information, including:

- Secondary School Certificate (SSC) and Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) examination roll numbers

- Education boards

2. Personal details

Applicants must provide the following information:

- Language of the question paper and answer script (the language in which they wish to take the admission test)

- Present address

- Mobile phone number and email address (both must be personal)

- National identity card numbers of parents (optional) and their occupations

- Quota information, if applicable (details are available in the admission guidelines)

- The unit in which they wish to take the admission test

3. Photograph

Applicants must upload a photograph meeting the following specifications:

- Minimum width: 450 pixels

- Minimum height: 550 pixels

- File size: 20KB

- Format: .jpg or .jpeg

- Background: Plain white

4. Password

Applicants can send an SMS using mobile connections from Teletalk, Banglalink, Grameenphone, Robi or Airtel.

They must use their own personal mobile phone numbers for this process.

5. Payment of fees

Finally, applicants must pay the application fee. Payment can be made through mobile financial services, internet banking, debit or credit cards.

Applicants can also pay through Sonali Bank, Agrani Bank, Janata Bank and Rupali Bank.

item.title: Petrol bomb thrown at Khulna City Corporation building
item.description:
Miscreants have thrown a petrol bomb targeting the Khulna City Corporation (KCC) building. At around 12:30 am early on Monday, the petrol bomb was thrown from the road outside the building on KD Ghosh Road in the city, aimed at its staircase.

Police said two young men arrived in front of the city corporation building on a motorcycle at around 12:30 am. They then threw the petrol bomb towards the staircase and quickly left the scene. The bomb landed on the stairs and exploded, causing a fire that burned for a short while before going out on its own.

CCTV footage from the city corporation building shows an object being thrown towards the building from the road in front. It landed on the staircase and exploded, and the fire went out shortly afterwards.

What do police officials think about crude bomb explosions, bus arson attacks?

Mohammad Lokman Hossain, officer-in-charge (OC) of Khulna Sadar police station, said police went to the scene after receiving information about the incident. The petrol bomb landed on the staircase of the city corporation building.

There was no major damage, although it left a slight mark on the stairs. The bomb was thrown by two young men who arrived on a motorcycle. Evidence was collected from the scene. Efforts are under way to identify and arrest those involved in the incident, he added.

Khulna City Corporation Administrator Nazrul Islam Manju visited the site where a petrol bomb was thrown at the city corporation building on Monday morning. Speaking to journalists at around 10:30 am, he said, “The city corporation is a service-oriented institution. We are shocked by the incident in which a bomb was thrown there.”

Vehicles set on fire, crude bomb explosions: What message IGP sends to SPs

“A criminal group, miscreants or collaborators of fascism may have thrown the bomb to spread panic among city residents or create fear and further unrest. Alongside the Metropolitan Police, Khulna City Corporation will form a separate investigation committee. CCTV footage from the surrounding area is being reviewed,” he added.

The city corporation administrator also said that AI-powered CCTV cameras would be installed as soon as possible to help maintain law and order in Khulna city. The police and the city corporation would work together to complete the task.

The initiative would be implemented for the people of Khulna very soon. He said that public concern over the law and order situation in Khulna was growing with each passing day. The prime minister has said that he would do whatever was necessary to ensure the safety of Khulna’s residents.
